children: Warsh revived US rate-hike bets, oil jumped above $90 and the yen surrendered most of its intervention gains. Tokyo’s line in the sand is looking distinctly sandy.
Yen crosses the danger zone
The
pair edged above ¥160 Monday for the first time since the
, reviving speculation that Tokyo and Washington could support the yen again. The pair previously climbed near ¥164 before official buying drove it as low as ¥155.20.

Japan spent a record ¥15.4 trillion — roughly $96.5 billion — supporting its currency between July 30 and August 26. The US Treasury also participated in the intervention, adding credibility to the move. One month later, most of that hard-purchased appreciation has already evaporated.
Immediate resistance sits around ¥160.50, followed by ¥162 and July’s
Support appears around ¥159, then ¥157.50 and the intervention low near ¥155. A rapid reversal below ¥160 would suggest official warnings are already influencing positioning.
Rate gap favors the dollar

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at Jackson Hole said policymakers still “have work to do” unless inflation moves convincingly toward 2%. Markets raised the probability of a September US rate increase to roughly 57%, pushing the rate-sensitive two-year Treasury yield to a one-month high near 4.33%.
The Bank of Japan’s policy rate remains around 1%, leaving US short-term yields more than three percentage points higher.
That gap encourages the carry trade — borrowing low-yielding yen to purchase higher-yielding dollar assets. Profitable, until an intervention candle reorganizes a quiet afternoon.
The BOJ may raise rates at its September meeting as inflation and yen weakness intensify pressure for faster tightening.

Japanese government bond yields are already elevated, however, limiting policymakers’ room. Higher domestic rates could support the yen while making Japan’s enormous government debt considerably costlier.
Oil adds another headache

Brent jumped above $90 after US strikes on Iran’s Larak Island triggered retaliation against American forces. Japan imports most of its energy, so higher oil increases its import bill and demand for dollars.
Despite the dollar-yen crossing ¥160, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described recent moves as orderly and “pretty well contained.”

That lowers the probability of immediate coordinated action. Authorities generally intervene against excessive volatility, not merely because traders have reached an aesthetically unpleasant round number.
Friday’s US payrolls report now becomes the next major catalyst. Economists expect 58,000 new jobs after July’s 23,000 decline.
Stronger hiring could push the exchange rate toward its previous highs; another weak report may lower Fed hike expectations and accomplish some of Tokyo’s work free of charge.
